c.tagline: Sand-swept Sahara capital where the desert meets the Atlantic.

taxi.fareNote: Shared 'taxi collectif' rides follow fixed per-seat fares by route; private 'course' rides have no meter and must be negotiated with the driver before departure.

emergency.medical: 18 (fire/ambulance - Protection Civile); private clinics recommended for serious cases
emergency.note: Emergency response is limited outside major hospitals; many expats use private clinics (e.g., Clinique Najah, Polyclinique) rather than relying on ambulance dispatch.

avoid.reason: Avoid the beaches and Port de Pêche area after dark and isolated outskirts, and skip overland travel to the north and east where terrorism risk is high.
Pickpocketing occurs in the Marché Capitale and Cinquième market crowds; avoid walking alone at night and keep documents copied.

hood_desc: Nouakchott's diplomatic and business quarter, lined with embassies, banks, upscale restaurants and the city's best hotels; suits business travelers, expats and anyone wanting comfort and easy taxi access.

The historic old town and administrative core around the Grande Mosquée and central market streets; suits budget-to-midrange travelers who want to be near sights, transport links and everyday Mauritanian street life.

A vast, chaotic commercial district built around the sprawling Sebkha market, one of West Africa's largest informal markets; suits adventurous budget travelers wanting an authentic, gritty local experience.
A large residential area known for its artisan and craft market (Marché Arafat); suits longer-stay visitors and those wanting a quieter, more local residential feel away from the center.

A quieter southern district near the Atlantic corniche and government buildings, with wide sandy streets and sea breezes; suits travelers wanting some distance from downtown noise and easy beach walks.

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for visitors; use bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Shared taxis are paid in cash (ouguiya) directly to the driver at a fixed per-seat fare set by route; the new STP BHNS express buses launched in 2025 use fixed fares collected on boarding, with card/prepaid ticketing being phased in. Private taxi rides ('course') should be agreed with the driver before departure since meters are not used.
transit.hours: Shared taxis and buses generally run from around 6:00am to 11:00pm; there is no organized night transit, so travelers arrange private taxis directly after dark.
transit.note: Nouakchott has no metro, tram or rail transit; most residents rely on informal shared taxis, supplemented since May 2025 by the city's first modern bus rapid transit (BHNS) network on dedicated lanes.

bus: Gare routière de Nouakchott (intercity coaches to Nouadhibou, Rosso, Kaédi, Néma and other regions)

transit.m: Private/shared taxi (30-40 min, no public bus link)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% is appreciated at restaurants frequented by tourists and expats, but not expected at local eateries or in taxis.

food.name: Thieboudienne
food.desc: The national dish - Atlantic fish stuffed with herb paste, simmered with vegetables and served over rice cooked in the tomato broth.

places.name: TATA Restaurant
places.note: Best-known address in the city for West African stews and a proper thieboudienne.

places.name: Le Maquis
places.note: Casual restaurant serving authentic Mauritanian and West African home cooking.

places.name: Port de Peche eateries
places.note: Cook-shops beside the fishing beach build the dish around whatever landed that morning.

food.name: Mechoui
food.desc: Whole lamb or a shoulder rubbed with salt and spice and roasted slowly over embers until the fat crisps - the centrepiece of Mauritanian hospitality.

places.name: Le Prince
places.note: Mauritanian-Moroccan kitchen that handles roast and grilled lamb well.

places.name: Restaurant Merzouga
places.note: North African menu with roast lamb and tagines in a comfortable setting.

places.name: Le Qasr
places.note: Upscale dining room where mechoui-style roasts are served for groups.

food.name: Grilled Atlantic Fish
food.desc: Whole capitaine, sole or dorade split, marinated and grilled over coals with onion sauce - Nouakchott's cold Atlantic current makes the fish exceptional.

places.name: Port de Peche fish grills
places.note: Pick your fish off the pirogues and have it grilled on the spot - the city's signature meal.

places.name: Restaurant la Mediterranee
places.note: Popular with locals and expats for fresh seafood and grilled fish.

places.name: Le Maquis
places.note: Reliable, unfussy kitchen for grilled fish with rice or chips.

food.name: Maru We Lahm
food.desc: Rice cooked with camel or lamb, carrot, cabbage and pumpkin in a spiced broth, then piled onto a communal platter and eaten with the right hand.

places.name: TATA Restaurant
places.note: Serves the national repertoire of rice-and-meat platters as locals eat them.

places.name: Marche Capitale food stalls
places.note: Market kitchens dish up rice and meat by the plate at midday.

places.name: Le Maquis
places.note: Everyday Mauritanian plates including camel and lamb with rice.

food.name: Mauritanian Couscous
food.desc: Coarse couscous steamed over a broth of lamb or camel with pumpkin, carrot and chickpeas, finished with buttermilk or a spoon of ghee.

places.name: Restaurant Merzouga
places.note: Maghrebi kitchen where couscous is a standing weekly special.

places.name: Le Prince
places.note: Blends Mauritanian and Moroccan cooking, couscous included.

places.name: Marche Sixieme food stalls
places.note: Busy market district where cheap kitchens serve couscous to local workers.

food.name: Lakh
food.desc: Millet or maize couscous stirred into soured milk and sugar, sometimes with baobab or peanut - a cooling everyday breakfast and supper.

places.name: Marche Capitale
places.note: Women sell fresh lakh and soured-milk dishes from bowls at the market.

places.name: Marche Sixieme
places.note: Milk and millet vendors work the market lanes from early morning.

places.name: TATA Restaurant
places.note: Keeps West African millet and milk desserts on the menu.

food.name: Zrig
food.desc: Camel or goat milk thinned with water and lightly sweetened, served cold - the drink Mauritanians offer guests first. No alcohol is sold here.

places.name: Marche Capitale milk sellers
places.note: Fresh camel milk and zrig sold by the bottle from coolers each morning.

places.name: Marche Sixieme
places.note: Camel-milk vendors are a fixture of this large local market.

places.name: TATA Restaurant
places.note: Serves zrig and other traditional non-alcoholic drinks with meals.

food.name: Attaya Mint Tea
food.desc: Green tea boiled with sugar and mint and poured from height into small glasses across three rounds, each stronger and sweeter than the last.

places.name: Sahara Cafe
places.note: Comfortable cafe for tea and pastries without hunting down a street brazier.

places.name: Marche Capitale tea stalls
places.note: Tea braziers set up in the market lanes; the full three-glass ritual for pocket change.

places.name: Le Prince
places.note: Finishes meals with the traditional foamed mint tea service.

landmarks: Saudi Mosque (Grande Mosquée Saoudienne)
Nouakchott's largest and most prominent mosque, a gift from Saudi Arabia whose soaring minaret and green-domed silhouette anchor the capital's skyline.
Cathédrale Saint-Joseph
The modest yet striking Catholic cathedral of Mauritania's capital, notable as a rare Christian landmark in this predominantly Muslim desert nation.
Marché Capitale
The capital's central market is a vibrant maze of vendors selling textiles, jewelry, and Saharan crafts, offering an immersive taste of Mauritanian daily commerce.
Port de Pêche (Fishermen's Beach)
A mesmerizing, chaotic shoreline crowded with hundreds of brightly painted wooden pirogues, where fishermen haul in the day's catch amid swirling seabirds.
National Museum of Mauritania
A compact but rich museum tracing Mauritania's nomadic heritage, Saharan archaeology, and traditional crafts through well-curated regional collections.
Nouakchott Camel Market
A dusty, atmospheric marketplace on the city's edge where herders trade camels amid haggling and dust clouds, an unforgettable slice of Saharan life.
Stade Olympique de Nouakchott
Mauritania's national stadium hosts football matches and major public events, serving as a modern gathering point and symbol of the country's sporting ambitions.
Nouakchott Beach
A wide expanse of Atlantic coastline where locals stroll at dusk and fishing boats line the sand, offering a relaxed contrast to the desert capital's dusty streets.
Sebkha District
A sprawling, low-lying salt-flat neighborhood on the city's western edge, known for its distinct desert-meets-urban landscape and everyday Mauritanian street life.
Nouakchott–Oumtounsy International Airport
The gleaming gateway to Mauritania, this modern airport terminal is often visitors' first striking glimpse of the country's blend of tradition and ambition.

train.note: Mauritania's only railway is the iron-ore line between Nouadhibou and Zouerat (about 700 km north). It carries a single free passenger car but does not serve Nouakchott - to ride it you must first get to Nouadhibou or Zouerat. No rail from the capital.

bus.note: No international coach with online booking runs from Nouakchott. To Dakar (Senegal), shared sept-place taxis and minibuses cross at the Rosso river ferry (or the Diama dam) border. Toward Dakhla and Morocco, buses and 4x4s cross the Guerguerat border in the far north. Long-distance domestic buses leave from the Garage areas in town; carry your passport.

ferry.note: No passenger ferries. Nouakchott's Port de l'Amitie handles cargo and fishing only.

full.name: Saint-Louis
full.blurb: Historic former colonial capital known for its island setting and colorful architecture.
